passages.original: Tale initium fuit Dionis et Dionysii simultatis, eaque multis rebus aucta est. sed tamen primis temporibus aliquamdiu simulata inter eos amicitia mansit. sicut, cum Dion non desisteret obsecrare Dionysium, ut Platonem Athenis arcesseret et eius consiliis uteretur, ille, qui in aliqua re vellet patrem imitari, morem ei gessit. eodemque tempore Philistum historicum Syracusas reduxit, hominem amicum non magis tyranno quam tyrannidi.
passages.english: Such was the beginning of the enmity between Dion and Dionysius, and it was increased by many things. But nevertheless in the early period a feigned friendship remained between them for some time. So, when Dion did not cease to entreat Dionysius to summon Plato from Athens and make use of his counsels, Dionysius, who wished to imitate his father in some respect, humoured him. And at the same time he brought the historian Philistus back to Syracuse, a man who was no more a friend to the tyrant than to tyranny.

passages.original: deinde orta dissensio est inter eum et Heraclidem, qui, quod ei principatum non concedebat, factionem comparavit. neque is minus valebat apud optimates, quorum consensu praeerat classi, cum Dion exercitum pedestrem teneret. non tulit hoc animo aequo Dion, et versum illum Homeri rettulit ex secunda rhapsodia, in quo haec sententia est: non posse bene geri rem publicam multorum imperiis. quod dictum magna invidia consecuta est: namque aperuisse videbatur omnia in sua potestate esse velle.
passages.english: Then a quarrel arose between him and Heraclides, who, because he would not concede the leading position to him, formed a faction. Nor did he have less influence among the aristocrats, by whose consent he commanded the fleet, while Dion held the land army. Dion did not bear this calmly, and he quoted that line of Homer from the second book, in which there is this sentiment: that a state cannot be well governed under the rule of many. This saying was followed by great ill will, for he seemed to have revealed that he wanted everything to be in his own power.
passages.notes: The Homeric line is Iliad 2.204 ("the rule of many is not good"); Latin 'rhapsodia' refers to a book of the Iliad.
